verses.text: Yahweh’s word came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha, saying,

“Because I exalted you out of the dust, and made you prince over my people Israel, and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam, and have made my people Israel to sin, to provoke me to anger with their sins;
behold, I will utterly sweep away Baasha and his house; and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat.
The dogs will eat Baasha’s descendants who die in the city; and he who dies of his in the field, the birds of the sky will eat.”
Now the rest of the acts of Baasha, and what he did, and his might, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
Baasha slept with his fathers, and was buried in Tirzah; and Elah his son reigned in his place.

Moreover Yahweh’s word came by the prophet Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha and against his house, both because of all the evil that he did in Yahweh’s sight, to provoke him to anger with the work of his hands, in being like the house of Jeroboam, and because he struck him.
In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah the son of Baasha began to reign over Israel in Tirzah for two years.
His servant Zimri, captain of half his chariots, conspired against him. Now he was in Tirzah, drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza, who was over the household in Tirzah;
and Zimri went in and struck him, and killed him, in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned in his place.
When he began to reign, as soon as he sat on his throne, he attacked all the house of Baasha. He didn’t leave him a single one who urinates on a wall  among his relatives or his friends.
Thus Zimri destroyed all the house of Baasha, according to Yahweh’s word, which he spoke against Baasha by Jehu the prophet,
for all the sins of Baasha, and the sins of Elah his son, which they sinned, and with which they made Israel to sin, to provoke Yahweh, the God of Israel, to anger with their vanities.
Now the rest of the acts of Elah, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned seven days in Tirzah. Now the people were encamped against Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines.
The people who were encamped heard that Zimri had conspired, and had also killed the king. Therefore all Israel made Omri, the captain of the army, king over Israel that day in the camp.
Omri went up from Gibbethon, and all Israel with him, and they besieged Tirzah.
When Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the fortified part of the king’s house, and burned the king’s house over him with fire, and died,
for his sins which he sinned in doing that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, in walking in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin which he did, to make Israel to sin.
Now the rest of the acts of Zimri, and his treason that he committed, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
Then the people of Israel were divided into two parts: half of the people followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king; and half followed Omri.
But the people who followed Omri prevailed against the people who followed Tibni the son of Ginath; so Tibni died, and Omri reigned.
In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri began to reign over Israel for twelve years. He reigned six years in Tirzah.
He bought the hill Samaria of Shemer for two talents  of silver; and he built on the hill, and called the name of the city which he built Samaria, after the name of Shemer, the owner of the hill.
Omri did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, and dealt wickedly above all who were before him.
For he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and in his sins with which he made Israel to sin, to provoke Yahweh, the God of Israel, to anger with their vanities.
Now the rest of the acts of Omri which he did, and his might that he showed, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
So Omri slept with his fathers, and was buried in Samaria; and Ahab his son reigned in his place.
In the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah, Ahab the son of Omri began to reign over Israel. Ahab the son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty-two years.
Ahab the son of Omri did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight above all that were before him.

As if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, he took as wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and went and served Baal, and worshiped him.
He raised up an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he had built in Samaria.
Ahab made the Asherah; and Ahab did more yet to provoke Yahweh, the God of Israel, to anger than all the kings of Israel who were before him.

In his days Hiel the Bethelite built Jericho. He laid its foundation with the loss of Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates with the loss of his youngest son Segub, according to Yahweh’s word, which he spoke by Joshua the son of Nun.

footnotes.content: Here comes the word of the Lord through Jehu the prophet—a hard word, yes, but spoken. When we stray, the Lord doesn't go silent. He sends His witness, even when His witness will not be welcomed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baasha rose from nothing, exalted by grace—yet walked in Jeroboam's footsteps, leading Israel into the very sins the Lord called him to escape. How easily we forget the mercies that lifted us, and repeat the ruin we fled.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord will sweep away house and dynasty. It's not cruelty; it's the gravity of unfaithfulness. We cannot toy with sin and expect the Lord to merely scold us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Dogs and birds eating the dead—an ancient shame, the opposite of proper burial and honor. Yet even in judgment, the Lord uses the very creation to witness that there are consequences to forsaking Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A king's acts and might, all written and then forgotten. What men record as achievement often amounts to little when weighed against faithfulness to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baasha sleeps with his fathers in Tirzah. The city was his capital, yet his rest there tells us nothing of his peace with God. Burial is not vindication.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The prophet names the Lord's reason clearly: Baasha provoked the Lord by doing evil, and by striking down Nadab to seize the throne. Even when He judges, the Lord is just—nothing is hidden from Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elah reigns, son of Baasha, in Tirzah. Two years is all his reign will last. How little time to squander what was seized by violence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zimri, a captain of chariots, conspires while Elah drinks in drunken ease. The servant rises against the master, heedless of tomorrow. How often does pride and pleasure leave a throne unguarded.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One stroke, and the reign of Baasha's house ends. Zimri killed the king and took the throne for himself—but his reign will prove even shorter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zimri annihilates the entire house of Baasha—no man left standing. Vengeance seeks its own, and one conspiracy begets another. The violence is breathtaking and dreadful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet in Zimri's rage, the Lord's word through Jehu comes to pass. His judgment flows through the wickedness of men, their plans unknowing, their hands His instrument.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The root sin named: both Baasha and Elah walked in the way of Jeroboam, their vanities provoked the Lord. One man's idolatry corrupted generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again, the formula: Elah's acts written, then forgotten. Israel's chronicles fill with kings of little moment—yet not forgotten by the Lord, who sees all and remembers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven days Zimri reigns in Tirzah—a brevity that mirrors his haste and his doom. Meanwhile Israel's army camps against Gibbethon, far away, and the kingdom fractures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The army hears that Zimri conspired and killed the king. Swift as thought, they crown Omri their captain. Power flows like water, seeking its level, caring nothing for the man swept aside.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Omri marches on Tirzah with all Israel at his back. Zimri's usurped throne already crumbles beneath him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zimri sees the city taken, runs into the king's house, and burns it over himself. A death by his own hand rather than the enemy's—pride's last defiant stroke before the void.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The cause is named: Zimri too walked in Jeroboam's way and made Israel to sin. He was not merely ambitious; he was unfaithful. His end was not mere politics—it was judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His treason is written in the chronicles, then forgotten by the world. Yet the Lord forgets nothing—Zimri's name lives on, a monument to the wages of pride and conspiracy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel splits in two, half following Tibni, half following Omri. The kingdom tears itself apart over rival claims, and the Lord allows it—judgment through their own divisions.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Omri's followers prevail; Tibni dies. Omri takes the throne whole. But the kingdom has been weakened by its own civil war—no victor emerges unscathed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Omri reigns twelve years, the last six in Tirzah. His reign stabilizes, but the text will show us it is built on faithlessness, not faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Omri buys the hill Samaria and builds a city there, naming it after the former owner. It becomes Israel's new capital—a great city, but built by a man estranged from the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Evil in the Lord's sight, dealing wickedly above all before him. Omri's ambition and architectural achievement cannot hide his spiritual ruin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He walked in Jeroboam's way, the same path every unfaithful king takes—idolatry, provocation of the Lord. The sins replicate, each reign copying the last.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His might is written in the chronicles—all his deeds, his building of Samaria, his twelve years of rule. Yet it is all dust, forgotten by the Lord who sees his heart unfaithful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Omri sleeps with his fathers and is buried in Samaria, the city he built. His tomb will be in his greatest work—yet he goes to his grave estranged from the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahab, Omri's son, begins his reign—and the text pauses to tell us he reigned twenty-two years. A long reign is coming, and it will carry Israel into darkness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahab did evil in the Lord's sight above all before him. The trajectory is set: each king outpaces the last in unfaithfulness, descending deeper into darkness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahab marries Jezebel, daughter of the Sidonian king, and serves Baal. A marriage sealed in idolatry—he yokes himself to a woman and a god that will bring Israel to ruin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An altar to Baal in Samaria, the royal city. Apostasy becomes official; the king himself leads the people into worship of a demon god.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in how quickly a kingdom can lose its way. Ahab's choice to provoke the Lord more than all the kings before him shows how one leader's unfaithfulness can poison a whole generation—a warning as old as kingdoms themselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hiel rebuilds Jericho, and his sons die in the foundation and gates—the curse from Joshua's day comes to pass. The word of the Lord spoken generations before is still alive, still true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
